fp1_induction_sums.description: Verify the first case, derive the next claim from the assumption and write a conclusion covering the stated integer range.

sections.title: Which case starts an induction proof?
sections.label: Use the smallest admissible index
sections.intro: Read the range of integers in the claim. Evaluate both sides of the first allowed case independently.

blocks.html: A proof starts where the claim starts. The smallest index can be zero, one or a later integer.

blocks.title: Connect the exact starting case to a new summand
blocks.prompt: The claim is \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(3 r + 4\right)\) equal to \(\frac{n \left(3 n + 11\right)}{2}\) for every integer n from \(1\) onwards. Give the starting index and the common value of both sides at that index.
blocks.hint: Write the claim at k and at k + 1, then compare what their left sides differ by.
blocks.solution:
At \(n=1\) the left side has a single term, equal to \(7\). The proposed formula gives the same value.

Assume the formula at \(n=k\). The next sum adds the term at \(k+1\), which is \(3 k + 7\).

Adding that term to the assumed expression gives \(\frac{\left(k + 1\right) \left(3 k + 14\right)}{2}\), as required. The base and step establish the claim on its stated interval.

blocks.html: Matching the two sides for one index starts the proof. It does not establish the step.

sections.title: Why do I state the claim at an arbitrary k?
sections.label: Separate the two claims
sections.intro: Assume the statement at any allowed k. Your proof must show this assumption is enough to obtain the next statement.

blocks.html: For a sum, the next left-hand side is the old sum plus the term with index k + 1. Replace the old sum by the assumed formula.

blocks.title: Connect the exact starting case to a new summand
blocks.prompt: The claim is \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(3 r + 4\right)\right)\) equal to \(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 5\right)}{2}\) for every integer n from \(1\) onwards. Give the added term as a polynomial in k and the value of both sides in the base case.

fields.label: Added term as a polynomial in k

blocks.hint: Write the claim at k and at k + 1, then compare what their left sides differ by.
blocks.solution:
At \(n=1\) the left side has a single term, equal to \(7\). The proposed formula gives the same value.

Assume the formula at \(n=k\). The next sum adds the term at \(k+1\), which is \(3 k^{2} + 10 k + 7\).

Adding that term to the assumed expression gives \(\frac{\left(k + 1\right) \left(k + 2\right) \left(2 k + 7\right)}{2}\), as required. The base and step establish the claim on its stated interval.

blocks.html: Do not use the result at k + 1 as an assumption while trying to prove it.

sections.title: How do I handle a sum that starts later than one?
sections.label: Retain the original lower limit
sections.intro: The lower limit stays fixed throughout the induction. At the first index the sum contains its first term only.

blocks.html: Keep the given lower index when writing both the base case and the step. Only the upper limit changes.

blocks.title: Connect the exact starting case to a new summand
blocks.prompt: The claim is \(\sum_{r=4}^{n}\left(3 r + 4\right)\) equal to \(\frac{\left(n - 3\right) \left(3 n + 20\right)}{2}\) for every integer n from \(4\) onwards. Give the base index and the next summand as a polynomial in k.

fields.label: Added term as a polynomial in k

blocks.hint: Write the claim at k and at k + 1, then compare what their left sides differ by.
blocks.solution:
At \(n=4\) the left side has a single term, equal to \(16\). The proposed formula gives the same value.

Assume the formula at \(n=k\). The next sum adds the term at \(k+1\), which is \(3 k + 7\).

Adding that term to the assumed expression gives \(\frac{\left(k - 2\right) \left(3 k + 23\right)}{2}\), as required. The base and step establish the claim on its stated interval.

blocks.html: If you replace a late starting index with one, you prove a different sum.

blocks.title: Connect the exact starting case to a new summand
blocks.prompt: The claim is \(\sum_{r=6}^{n}\left(5 r + 6\right)\) equal to \(\frac{\left(n - 5\right) \left(5 n + 42\right)}{2}\) for every integer n from \(6\) onwards. Give the base index and the next summand as a polynomial in k.

fields.label: Added term as a polynomial in k

blocks.hint: Write the claim at k and at k + 1, then compare what their left sides differ by.
blocks.solution:
At \(n=6\) the left side has a single term, equal to \(36\). The proposed formula gives the same value.

Assume the formula at \(n=k\). The next sum adds the term at \(k+1\), which is \(5 k + 11\).

Adding that term to the assumed expression gives \(\frac{\left(k - 4\right) \left(5 k + 47\right)}{2}\), as required. The base and step establish the claim on its stated interval.

sections.title: What else is needed when the claim is an inequality?
sections.label: Compare with the new target
sections.intro: Use the assumed inequality only with valid operations. Multiplying by a positive number preserves its direction.

blocks.html: After applying the assumption, show that the new bound is at least or at most the desired next quantity as required.

blocks.title: Bridge an inequality rather than only an equality
blocks.prompt: To prove \(3^n\ge n+1\) for all \(n\ge0\), assume it at \(n=k\). State the multiplier on the assumption and the excess of this resulting lower bound over \(k+2\) at \(k=3\).
blocks.hint: Prove the derived bound is at least the next target, rather than assuming it.
blocks.solution:
At n zero both sides are one.

Multiply the inductive assumption by the positive number \(3\). The next power is then at least \(3 k + 3\).

Its difference from the target \(k+2\) is \(2 k + 1\), non-negative for every allowed k. This proves the induction step. At the specified k it is \(7\).

blocks.html: A derived inequality may be too weak. Check the final comparison explicitly.

sections.title: How can a proposed formula match several cases and still be false?
sections.label: Search for a counterexample
sections.intro: A finite set of matching cases need not imply any later case. An extra factor can vanish at every tested index.

blocks.html: One counterexample disproves a universal claim. An induction step must establish a real implication rather than report more tests.

blocks.title: Find a counterexample after several successful checks
blocks.prompt: For the sum of the first n odd numbers, someone proposes \(2 n^{4} - 20 n^{3} + 71 n^{2} - 100 n + 48\). Find the first positive n where this fails and the amount by which the proposed formula exceeds the correct sum.
blocks.hint: Check where all correction factors are non-zero for the first time.
blocks.solution:
For the first four positive indices the correction product has a zero factor.

The usual odd sum is \(n^2\). It starts at one and increases by \(2k+1\) between \(k\) and \(k+1\), giving the induction step.

At five the proposed correction is \(48\), which is non-zero. This is the first failure.

blocks.html: Testing four or five values is useful checking, but cannot replace the induction step.

glossary.definition: First verified case of the statement.
Assumption of the claim at an arbitrary allowed index.
Argument that the next claim follows from the hypothesis.
Specific value for which a proposed claim fails.
Statement that links the base and step to all allowed indices.

revision.body:
Choose the next step

SituationMethod
BaseCheck the first allowed index on both sides.
AssumeState the claim at an arbitrary allowed k.
StepUse the assumption to derive the claim at k + 1.
ConcludeGive the integer range reached from the verified start.

Try a quick check

When proving a sum to n, what one term is added to reach the sum to k + 1 from the sum to k?

Check The summand at index \(r=k+1\).

fp1_induction_derivatives.description: Follow the derivative order through constant, chain and product-rule steps, and handle cycles in a block of derivatives.

sections.title: What does derivative order zero mean?
sections.label: Start with the original function
sections.intro: Order zero means no differentiation has been applied. It is the original function.

blocks.html: At each next order, differentiate the assumed formula with respect to x, with the index held constant.

blocks.title: Carry a constant multiplier through one derivative
blocks.prompt: For \(y=e^{3 x + 4}\), give the multiplier when passing from the kth to the next derivative, and the coefficient of y in the derivative of order \(3\).
blocks.hint: The derivative of the exponent is a constant. Keep track of how many times it is applied.
blocks.solution:
At order zero the expression is y itself.

Differentiating multiplies y by \(3\) and leaves its form unchanged. Thus each step introduces the same multiplier.

Induction gives coefficient \(3^k\) at order k. At the requested order it is \(27\).

blocks.html: If the claim starts at order zero, starting with the first derivative omits its actual base case.

sections.title: Which factor comes from the inner expression?
sections.label: Use the chain rule with the current exponent
sections.intro: For a power of a linear expression, differentiation multiplies by the current exponent and by the derivative of the expression inside.

blocks.html: State both the new coefficient and the exponent after applying the chain rule. A negative power decreases by one.

blocks.title: Track the power shift and chain factor
blocks.prompt: For \(y=\frac{1}{3 x + 4}\) on \(3 x + 4>0\), give the signed coefficient and the exponent of \(3 x + 4\) in derivative order \(3\).
blocks.hint: Retain both the current negative exponent and the derivative of the bracket.
blocks.solution:
At order zero the exponent is \(-1\) and the coefficient is one.

At order k, differentiation multiplies the coefficient by \(- 3 k - 3\) and subtracts one from the exponent.

Induction gives \((-3)^k\frac{(1+k-1)!}{(1-1)!}\left(3 x + 4\right)^{-1-k}\). At the requested order the coefficient is \(-162\) and the exponent is \(-4\).

blocks.html: A negative sign changes the coefficient. The exponent still moves one step lower.

sections.title: Why does a factorial appear in a repeated derivative?
sections.label: Track the running product
sections.intro: The magnitude of a negative exponent increases at each step. The corresponding sequence of multipliers accumulates into a product of consecutive integers.

blocks.html: Match the newly introduced integer factor to the next factorial quotient and keep the repeated linear chain factor.

blocks.title: Track the power shift and chain factor
blocks.prompt: For \(y=\frac{1}{\left(3 x + 4\right)^{3}}\) on \(3 x + 4>0\), give the signed coefficient and the exponent of \(3 x + 4\) in derivative order \(3\).
blocks.hint: Retain both the current negative exponent and the derivative of the bracket.
blocks.solution:
At order zero the exponent is \(-3\) and the coefficient is one.

At order k, differentiation multiplies the coefficient by \(- 3 k - 9\) and subtracts one from the exponent.

Induction gives \((-3)^k\frac{(3+k-1)!}{(3-1)!}\left(3 x + 4\right)^{-3-k}\). At the requested order the coefficient is \(-1620\) and the exponent is \(-6\).

blocks.html: Using the same exponent multiplier at every stage ignores how the exponent changes.

blocks.title: Track the power shift and chain factor
blocks.prompt: For \(y=\frac{1}{\left(5 x + 6\right)^{5}}\) on \(5 x + 6>0\), give the signed coefficient and the exponent of \(5 x + 6\) in derivative order \(5\).
blocks.hint: Retain both the current negative exponent and the derivative of the bracket.
blocks.solution:
At order zero the exponent is \(-5\) and the coefficient is one.

At order k, differentiation multiplies the coefficient by \(- 5 k - 25\) and subtracts one from the exponent.

Induction gives \((-5)^k\frac{(5+k-1)!}{(5-1)!}\left(5 x + 6\right)^{-5-k}\). At the requested order the coefficient is \(-47250000\) and the exponent is \(-10\).

sections.title: How can one induction step contain four differentiations?
sections.label: Count blocks consistently
sections.intro: Some functions return to the same trigonometric form after a fixed number of differentiations.

blocks.html: When n counts blocks, advance from one block index to the next using four actual derivatives in this example.

blocks.title: Use four differentiations as a single induction step
blocks.prompt: For \(y=\sin{\left(3 x \right)}\), let the index n count blocks of four differentiations. Give the block multiplier and the coefficient of y after \(8\) differentiations.
blocks.hint: An induction step of one block means four actual differentiations.
blocks.solution:
At zero blocks the function is unchanged. Differentiate four times: sine, cosine, minus sine, minus cosine, then sine.

Each differentiation introduces a factor \(3\). Thus one block gives multiplier \(81\).

A step from n blocks to n + 1 blocks applies the same multiplier once more. The requested coefficient is \(6561\).

blocks.html: The index of a block is not the raw derivative order.

sections.title: What does the product rule add at the next order?
sections.label: Carry the polynomial coefficient update
sections.intro: When the expression is an exponential times a polynomial, differentiating once produces two contributions.

blocks.html: Differentiate the exponential and the polynomial separately, then combine them into a recurrence for the remaining coefficients.

blocks.title: Keep the derivative of the polynomial factor
blocks.prompt: For \(y=\left(x - 4\right) e^{3 x}\), the derivative of order \(3\) equals \(\mathrm e^{3x}(Ax+B)\). Find \(A,B\).
blocks.hint: Apply the product rule to both factors. The derivative of the linear factor contributes to B.
blocks.solution:
Suppose order k has exponential times \(A_kx+B_k\). At order zero the coefficients are \(1,-4\).

The product rule gives \(A_{k+1}=3A_k\) and \(B_{k+1}=A_k+3B_k\).

Hence \(27 x - 81\) is the polynomial factor at the requested order. Its coefficients can also be checked by repeated differentiation.

blocks.html: Differentiating only the exponential misses the changing constant term.

blocks.title: Keep the derivative of the polynomial factor
blocks.prompt: For \(y=\left(x - 6\right) e^{5 x}\), the derivative of order \(5\) equals \(\mathrm e^{5x}(Ax+B)\). Find \(A,B\).
blocks.hint: Apply the product rule to both factors. The derivative of the linear factor contributes to B.
blocks.solution:
Suppose order k has exponential times \(A_kx+B_k\). At order zero the coefficients are \(1,-6\).

The product rule gives \(A_{k+1}=5A_k\) and \(B_{k+1}=A_k+5B_k\).

Hence \(3125 x - 15625\) is the polynomial factor at the requested order. Its coefficients can also be checked by repeated differentiation.

A step from n blocks to n + 1 blocks applies the same multiplier once more. The requested coefficient is \(16\).

examples.title: Keep the derivative of the polynomial factor
examples.question: For \(y=\left(x - 3\right) e^{2 x}\), the derivative of order \(2\) equals \(\mathrm e^{2x}(Ax+B)\). Find \(A,B\).
solution: Suppose order k has exponential times \(A_kx+B_k\). At order zero the coefficients are \(1,-3\).
The product rule gives \(A_{k+1}=2A_k\) and \(B_{k+1}=A_k+2B_k\).
Hence \(4 x - 8\) is the polynomial factor at the requested order. Its coefficients can also be checked by repeated differentiation.

Induction gives \((-4)^k\frac{(1+k-1)!}{(1-1)!}\left(4 x + 5\right)^{-1-k}\). At the requested order the coefficient is \(6144\) and the exponent is \(-5\).

extraPractice.solution:
At order zero the exponent is \(-6\) and the coefficient is one.

extraPractice.hint: An induction step of one block means four actual differentiations.
extraPractice.solution:
At zero blocks the function is unchanged. Differentiate four times: sine, cosine, minus sine, minus cosine, then sine.

Each differentiation introduces a factor \(4\). Thus one block gives multiplier \(256\).

A step from n blocks to n + 1 blocks applies the same multiplier once more. The requested coefficient is \(16777216\).

extraPractice.prompt: For \(y=\left(x - 7\right) e^{6 x}\), the derivative of order \(6\) equals \(\mathrm e^{6x}(Ax+B)\). Find \(A,B\).
extraPractice.hint: Apply the product rule to both factors. The derivative of the linear factor contributes to B.
extraPractice.solution:
Suppose order k has exponential times \(A_kx+B_k\). At order zero the coefficients are \(1,-7\).

The product rule gives \(A_{k+1}=6A_k\) and \(B_{k+1}=A_k+6B_k\).

Hence \(46656 x - 279936\) is the polynomial factor at the requested order. Its coefficients can also be checked by repeated differentiation.

fp1_induction_recurrences.description: Prove a recursive formula or bound by substituting the inductive assumption, with enough initial values.

sections.title: How do I use the given recursive rule in the proof?
sections.label: Substitute into the recurrence
sections.intro: The rule specifies the next term in terms of previous ones. The proposed formula must make that exact update.

blocks.html: Check the starting term, substitute the assumed formula and simplify to the stated next formula.

blocks.title: Substitute the assumed term into the recurrence
blocks.prompt: Let \(u_0=2\) and \(u_{n+1}=3u_n+5\). The proposed formula is \(u_n=\frac{9 \cdot 3^{n}}{2} - \frac{5}{2}\). Give the coefficient of \(3^n\) and the additive constant.
blocks.hint: Keep the constant when substituting the assumed formula into the recurrence.
blocks.solution:
The formula at zero gives the specified initial value.

Assume the formula at k. Multiplying by \(3\) and adding \(5\) turns its exponential part into the next power.

The constant stays \(- \frac{5}{2}\) because \(3(- \frac{5}{2})+5=- \frac{5}{2}\). This proves the formula by induction.

blocks.html: Testing only the proposed formula at a later input bypasses the recurrence.

sections.title: Why can adding a constant simplify a recurrence?
sections.label: Move to a geometric sequence
sections.intro: A fixed offset can hide a multiplicative recurrence. A shift of every term can remove the additive part.

blocks.html: Find an offset that makes the shifted new term a fixed multiple of the shifted old term.

blocks.title: Shift a recurrence to a pure geometric one
blocks.prompt: Given \(u_0=2\) and \(u_{n+1}=3(u_n+4)-4\), find \(u_1\) and the constant that must be added to each term so the shifted sequence is geometric.

fields.label: Value of the first term after the initial one

blocks.hint: Add the same offset to both successive terms.
blocks.solution:
Move the fixed offset to the same side as the next term.

Defining \(v_n=u_n+4\) gives \(v_{n+1}=3v_n\). Verify the shifted initial value.

By induction the shift follows geometric growth. At the first step the original term is \(14\).

blocks.html: Apply the same shift to both terms, including the initial value.

sections.title: When are two initial cases needed?
sections.label: Carry adjacent assumptions
sections.intro: If the next term requires the previous two terms, the inductive step must start from two known consecutive formulas.

blocks.html: Verify both base cases. Assume the pair at k and k + 1, prove the next formula and retain the last two.

blocks.title: Carry two consecutive assumptions through one step
blocks.prompt: For \(u_n=2 \left(-1\right)^{n} + 3 \cdot 2^{n}\), the rule is \(u_{n+2}=u_{n+1}+2u_n\). Give both required initial values and the coefficient multiplying u at index k in the induction step.

fields.label: Multiplier on u_k in the step

blocks.hint: This is a two-step recurrence, so checking just the first term cannot start the argument.
blocks.solution:
Two consecutive known values are needed. The formula at zero and one gives \(5\) and \(4\).

Assume both formulas at k and k + 1. The next term follows from \(u_{k+2}=u_{k+1}+2u_k\).

For the two exponential parts, the factors \(2\) and \(-1\) each satisfy \(q^2=q+2\), which proves the step.

blocks.html: One base value cannot generate the second without a separate condition in a two-step recursion.

blocks.title: Carry two consecutive assumptions through one step
blocks.prompt: For \(u_n=4 \left(-1\right)^{n} + 5 \cdot 2^{n}\), the rule is \(u_{n+2}=u_{n+1}+2u_n\). Give both required initial values and the coefficient multiplying u at index k in the induction step.

fields.label: Multiplier on u_k in the step

blocks.hint: This is a two-step recurrence, so checking just the first term cannot start the argument.
blocks.solution:
Two consecutive known values are needed. The formula at zero and one gives \(9\) and \(6\).

Assume both formulas at k and k + 1. The next term follows from \(u_{k+2}=u_{k+1}+2u_k\).

For the two exponential parts, the factors \(2\) and \(-1\) each satisfy \(q^2=q+2\), which proves the step.

sections.title: How can a recurrence preserve an interval?
sections.label: Check the range of the update
sections.intro: For a decreasing update map the largest permissible input gives the smallest image. Keep input denominators on the stated side of zero.

blocks.html: Show the whole image interval is inside the original interval, and check that the initial term is inside too.

blocks.title: Use both endpoints of an invariant interval
blocks.prompt: Let \(u_0=\frac{3}{2}\) and \(u_{n+1}=\frac{5}{3+u_n}\). Assuming \(1\le u_k\le2\), give the lower and upper bounds found for \(u_{k+1}\).

fields.label: Lower bound for the next term
Upper bound for the next term

blocks.hint: Check the denominator’s sign before reversing an inequality by taking reciprocals.
blocks.solution:
The initial value is between one and two. For the induction step the denominators are positive.

Taking reciprocals reverses the endpoints. Substitution at u equal to two gives the lower image \(1\), and at one gives the upper image \(\frac{5}{4}\).

The new interval is inside the original one, verifying that the same bound holds at k + 1.

blocks.html: Checking one test input does not prove that a whole interval is preserved.

sections.title: Can I test a proposed closed form by its differences?
sections.label: Compare consecutive values
sections.intro: For a recurrence that adds a function of the index, the difference between successive candidate values should equal that increment.

blocks.html: Match both the initial value and every symbolic increment to verify the proposed formula.

blocks.title: Use induction to verify a proposed closed form
blocks.prompt: The proposed formula is \(u_n=n^{2} + 3 n\) starting at zero. Give the starting value and the polynomial in k that the recurrence must add at each step.
blocks.hint: Subtract adjacent target expressions rather than guessing the increment.
blocks.solution:
At zero the formula gives zero.

Subtract the kth expression from the expression at k + 1, giving \(2 k + 4\).

Starting at zero and adding this expression each time establishes the proposed formula by induction.

blocks.html: A difference identity alone allows a constant error in every term. The starting value excludes that error.

fp1_induction_matrices.description: Prove matrix-power formulae using actual products, parity cycles and corrections that vanish at higher powers.

sections.title: Why are diagonal matrix powers straightforward?
sections.label: Apply powers to diagonal entries
sections.intro: Diagonal multiplication leaves all off-diagonal entries zero and acts independently on the diagonal.

blocks.html: Start with the identity at zero power. Multiply by the original matrix once to advance both diagonal powers.

blocks.title: Prove a power formula from multiplication on the diagonal
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 0\\0 & -4\end{matrix}\right]\), give the diagonal entries of \(A^{3}\).
blocks.hint: Use brackets around the negative base before applying its exponent.
blocks.solution:
At order zero the power is the identity. Each step multiplies the two diagonal entries separately by \(3\) and \(-4\).

Thus after n multiplications the leading entries are \(3^n\) and \((-4)^n\).

At the requested order the power is \(\left[\begin{matrix}27 & 0\\0 & -64\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: Negative diagonal bases need their signs raised to the same power.

sections.title: How do I prove a triangular entry grows linearly?
sections.label: Use its row–column product
sections.intro: A repeated shear can leave most matrix entries unchanged. One off-diagonal entry carries the accumulation.

blocks.html: Assume the matrix form at exponent k and show the next row–column products. The changing entry determines the new coefficient.

blocks.title: Track the single entry that changes at each power
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 3\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\), give the top-right entry of \(A^{3}\) and its increment per additional multiplication.
blocks.hint: Compute the first-row second-column product, keeping the diagonal ones.
blocks.solution:
At zero power the top-right entry is zero. Assume it is \(3k\) in the kth power.

Multiplication by A gives top-right entry \(3k+3\). The other entries match the old form.

This proves the general pattern and gives \(9\) at the requested order.

blocks.html: Checking the changing entry is useful only after the other entries have also been verified.

sections.title: What if powers alternate between two matrices?
sections.label: Check both parities
sections.intro: When squaring the matrix gives the identity, increasing the exponent by two leaves the power unchanged.

blocks.html: Prove each parity pattern from its own base case, or combine them into a paired induction statement.

blocks.title: Use a step of two for a matrix that repeats
blocks.prompt: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 3\\\frac{1}{3} & 0\end{matrix}\right]\), give the top-right entries of \(A^{6}\) and \(A^{7}\).

fields.label: Top-right entry at the even power
Top-right entry at the odd power

blocks.hint: Start once in each parity when the induction step advances by two.
blocks.solution:
Multiplying A by itself gives the identity. The two-step factor is therefore the identity at every stage.

At zero power the top-right entry is zero. At one power it is \(3\).

The even powers retain the first pattern and the odd powers retain the second.

blocks.html: A two-step proof starting at zero cannot prove the odd-index formula without another start.

blocks.title: Use a step of two for a matrix that repeats
blocks.prompt: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 5\\\frac{1}{5} & 0\end{matrix}\right]\), give the top-right entries of \(A^{10}\) and \(A^{11}\).

fields.label: Top-right entry at the even power
Top-right entry at the odd power

blocks.hint: Start once in each parity when the induction step advances by two.
blocks.solution:
Multiplying A by itself gives the identity. The two-step factor is therefore the identity at every stage.

At zero power the top-right entry is zero. At one power it is \(5\).

The even powers retain the first pattern and the odd powers retain the second.

sections.title: How can a vanishing cube simplify a three-by-three power?
sections.label: Track coefficients of J and J²
sections.intro: A correction matrix can have a non-zero square and a zero cube. Use the zero cube only after multiplying.

blocks.html: Compare the updated coefficients of the identity, the correction and its square. The last one gains the old linear coefficient at every step.

blocks.title: Keep the squared correction in a three-by-three power
blocks.prompt: Let \(J=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 3 & 0\\0 & 0 & 1\\0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(A=I+J\). Find the first-row third-column entries of \(J^2\) and \(A^{3}\).
blocks.hint: Preserve the J² term after multiplying and use J³ = 0 only where it applies.
blocks.solution:
The cube of J is zero. At power zero the proposed formula \(I+nJ+\frac12n(n-1)J^2\) is the identity.

Multiplying the formula at k by \(I+J\) adds one to the first coefficient and k to the second because the cubic term vanishes.

Thus the new quadratic coefficient matches \(\frac12k(k+1)\). The requested entries are \(3\) and \(9\).

blocks.html: Setting the square to zero when only the cube vanishes loses the quadratic term.

sections.title: How can a square-zero correction prove a power formula?
sections.label: Multiply and cancel the square
sections.intro: When a matrix is the identity plus a square-zero correction, each multiplication can add the correction once.

blocks.html: Verify the zero square directly. Then multiply the assumed formula by the original and check the resulting coefficient.

blocks.title: Recognise a matrix with a linear correction to identity
blocks.prompt: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}4 & -3\\3 & -2\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(N=A-I\). Find the top-left and top-right entries of \(A^{3}\).
blocks.hint: At the inductive step keep the product of the two correction terms until it can be shown zero.
blocks.solution:
Multiplication shows \(N^2=0\). The formula \(I+nN\) starts at the identity.

Assuming it at k, multiplication by \(I+N\) gives \(I+(k+1)N+kN^2\). The last term is zero.

This proves the power formula. The requested matrix is \(\left[\begin{matrix}10 & -9\\9 & -8\end{matrix}\right]\).

blocks.html: Do not assume a correction is square-zero just because the pattern worked for a different matrix.

blocks.title: Recognise a matrix with a linear correction to identity
blocks.prompt: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}6 & -5\\5 & -4\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(N=A-I\). Find the top-left and top-right entries of \(A^{5}\).
blocks.hint: At the inductive step keep the product of the two correction terms until it can be shown zero.

Multiplication shows \(N^2=0\). The formula \(I+nN\) starts at the identity.

Assuming it at k, multiplication by \(I+N\) gives \(I+(k+1)N+kN^2\). The last term is zero.

This proves the power formula. The requested matrix is \(\left[\begin{matrix}26 & -25\\25 & -24\end{matrix}\right]\).

Thus after n multiplications the leading entries are \(2^n\) and \((-3)^n\).
At the requested order the power is \(\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 0\\0 & 9\end{matrix}\right]\).

Multiplication by A gives top-right entry \(2k+2\). The other entries match the old form.
This proves the general pattern and gives \(4\) at the requested order.

examples.question: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 2\\\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{matrix}\right]\), give the top-right entries of \(A^{4}\) and \(A^{5}\).
solution: Multiplying A by itself gives the identity. The two-step factor is therefore the identity at every stage.

At order zero the power is the identity. Each step multiplies the two diagonal entries separately by \(4\) and \(-5\).

Thus after n multiplications the leading entries are \(4^n\) and \((-5)^n\).

At the requested order the power is \(\left[\begin{matrix}256 & 0\\0 & 625\end{matrix}\right]\).

extraPractice.title: Track the single entry that changes at each power
extraPractice.prompt: For \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 4\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]\), give the top-right entry of \(A^{4}\) and its increment per additional multiplication.
extraPractice.hint: Compute the first-row second-column product, keeping the diagonal ones.
extraPractice.solution:
At zero power the top-right entry is zero. Assume it is \(4k\) in the kth power.

Multiplication by A gives top-right entry \(4k+4\). The other entries match the old form.

This proves the general pattern and gives \(16\) at the requested order.

extraPractice.title: Use a step of two for a matrix that repeats
extraPractice.prompt: Given \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 6\\\frac{1}{6} & 0\end{matrix}\right]\), give the top-right entries of \(A^{12}\) and \(A^{13}\).

fields.label: Top-right entry at the even power
Top-right entry at the odd power

extraPractice.hint: Start once in each parity when the induction step advances by two.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiplying A by itself gives the identity. The two-step factor is therefore the identity at every stage.

At zero power the top-right entry is zero. At one power it is \(6\).

The even powers retain the first pattern and the odd powers retain the second.

extraPractice.title: Keep the squared correction in a three-by-three power
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(J=\left[\begin{matrix}0 & 4 & 0\\0 & 0 & 1\\0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(A=I+J\). Find the first-row third-column entries of \(J^2\) and \(A^{4}\).
extraPractice.hint: Preserve the J² term after multiplying and use J³ = 0 only where it applies.
extraPractice.solution:
The cube of J is zero. At power zero the proposed formula \(I+nJ+\frac12n(n-1)J^2\) is the identity.

Multiplying the formula at k by \(I+J\) adds one to the first coefficient and k to the second because the cubic term vanishes.

Thus the new quadratic coefficient matches \(\frac12k(k+1)\). The requested entries are \(4\) and \(24\).

extraPractice.title: Recognise a matrix with a linear correction to identity
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(A=\left[\begin{matrix}7 & -6\\6 & -5\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(N=A-I\). Find the top-left and top-right entries of \(A^{6}\).
extraPractice.hint: At the inductive step keep the product of the two correction terms until it can be shown zero.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiplication shows \(N^2=0\). The formula \(I+nN\) starts at the identity.

Assuming it at k, multiplication by \(I+N\) gives \(I+(k+1)N+kN^2\). The last term is zero.

This proves the power formula. The requested matrix is \(\left[\begin{matrix}37 & -36\\36 & -35\end{matrix}\right]\).

fp1_induction_divisibility.description: Carry integer multiples through expressions with products or powers. Choose an induction step that reaches the correct index set.

sections.title: How can a previous multiple establish the next one?
sections.label: Isolate a multiple of the assumed expression
sections.intro: Divisibility means equality to the divisor times an integer. Products by integers preserve divisibility.

blocks.html: Rewrite the next expression as an integer multiple of the previous one plus a new term divisible by the required divisor.

blocks.title: Keep a multiple of the previous expression visible
blocks.prompt: To prove that \(4\) divides \(5^{n} - 1\) for all non-negative integers n, write the next expression as \(aF_k+b\). Find \(a,b\).
blocks.hint: Subtract and add the same constant so that the earlier expression appears.
blocks.solution:
The base case is zero, which is a multiple of \(4\).

Write \(F_{k+1}=5F_k+4\). The first term is divisible by \(4\) if the inductive assumption holds, and the second is divisible directly.

The base and step establish the result for every non-negative integer.

blocks.html: Assuming a quotient is an integer is the conclusion you need to prove, not an available algebraic step.

sections.title: When is the difference easier than the next expression?
sections.label: Show the change is divisible
sections.intro: If the old expression and the change are both divisible by the same integer, their sum is divisible too.

blocks.html: Factor the change to expose consecutive integers or specific numerical factors.

blocks.title: Factor a difference of consecutive products
blocks.prompt: The claim is that \(\left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right) \left(n + 5\right)\) is divisible by six for all non-negative integers n. Give the base value and the expanded polynomial in k representing the change in the product from k to k + 1.
blocks.hint: Factor before expanding so the consecutive integers remain visible.
blocks.solution:
At zero the product is \(60\), divisible by six.

Factor the common two factors in the difference. This gives \(3 \left(k + 4\right) \left(k + 5\right)\).

The two consecutive integers in this factorisation give an even product. Multiplication by three makes the change divisible by six, carrying the divisibility forward.

blocks.html: Do not rely on checking a few numerical changes. The factor reasoning must hold at every admissible k.

sections.title: How do I rewrite a difference of powers for the induction step?
sections.label: Match one growth factor
sections.intro: The next expression has two exponential terms, each multiplied by its own base. Factor one base times the earlier expression.

blocks.html: The leftover contains a coefficient involving the difference of the bases; check it is a multiple of the divisor.

blocks.title: Use one growth factor to isolate the earlier powers
blocks.prompt: For \(F_n=- 3^{n} + 7^{n}\), write \(F_{k+1}=AF_k+B\). Give \(A\) and the value of \(B\) when \(k=2\). Use the form with B a constant times \(3^k\).
blocks.hint: Match one exponential term and factor the residual difference of bases.
blocks.solution:
The base value is zero, so it is divisible by \(4\).

Subtract \(7F_k\) from the next expression. The terms with the larger base cancel, leaving \(4 \cdot 3^{k}\).

This remainder is always a multiple of \(4\). At k equal to two it is \(36\). Thus the induction carries divisibility.

blocks.html: Use the earlier whole expression, including both terms and their signs.

blocks.title: Use one growth factor to isolate the earlier powers
blocks.prompt: For \(F_n=11^{n} - 5^{n}\), write \(F_{k+1}=AF_k+B\). Give \(A\) and the value of \(B\) when \(k=2\). Use the form with B a constant times \(5^k\).
blocks.hint: Match one exponential term and factor the residual difference of bases.
blocks.solution:
The base value is zero, so it is divisible by \(6\).

Subtract \(11F_k\) from the next expression. The terms with the larger base cancel, leaving \(6 \cdot 5^{k}\).

This remainder is always a multiple of \(6\). At k equal to two it is \(150\). Thus the induction carries divisibility.

sections.title: Why might the proof step need to add two?
sections.label: Advance to the next admissible integer
sections.intro: When the claim is only for odd integers, the next admissible index after k is k + 2.

blocks.html: Check the first positive odd integer and use an implication from an arbitrary odd k to k + 2.

blocks.title: Advance to the next eligible odd index
blocks.prompt: The claim is that eight divides \(n^{2} - 25\) for every positive odd integer n. Give the base value and the change in the expression when moving from \(k=3\) to the next odd index.

fields.label: Value at the first odd index

blocks.hint: A step of one would not stay within the set of odd indices.
blocks.solution:
The first index is one, giving \(-24\), a multiple of eight.

A step adds two to the index. The change is \(4(k+1)\). Since k is odd, k + 1 is even, so the change is divisible by eight.

At the requested k the change is \(16\). Thus the induction visits all positive odd integers.

blocks.html: A one-step induction cannot use an odd-only assumption at every integer.

sections.title: How do I prove divisibility by a square?
sections.label: Track the entire remainder
sections.intro: A linear correction to a power can remove the first-order contribution, leaving a multiple of a squared factor.

blocks.html: Subtract a suitable multiple of the preceding whole expression, then factor the remainder and compare with the squared divisor.

blocks.title: Carry a squared divisibility factor through the step
blocks.prompt: Let \(F_n=5^{n} - 4 n - 1\). In the form \(F_{k+1}=aF_k+ck\), find \(a,c\).
blocks.hint: Subtract a multiple of the whole earlier expression, including its constant and linear parts.
blocks.solution:
At zero the expression is zero.

Subtract \(5F_k\) from the next expression. The exponential terms cancel, leaving \(16 k\).

Because the remainder has the squared factor \(16\), induction proves divisibility by that factor.

blocks.html: Divisibility by a factor does not automatically prove divisibility by its square.

blocks.title: Carry a squared divisibility factor through the step
blocks.prompt: Let \(F_n=7^{n} - 6 n - 1\). In the form \(F_{k+1}=aF_k+ck\), find \(a,c\).
blocks.hint: Subtract a multiple of the whole earlier expression, including its constant and linear parts.
blocks.solution:
At zero the expression is zero.

Subtract \(7F_k\) from the next expression. The exponential terms cancel, leaving \(36 k\).

Because the remainder has the squared factor \(36\), induction proves divisibility by that factor.
